rationale: B wins because it separates the real stories instead of mashing the evidence problems into one overstuffed accountability angle. Its cleanest move is "Databricks graded its own model, and that is the part enterprises should check" - that is a real reporter-shaped critique with a concrete proof list. A has strong bones, but "Databricks claims $3B ARR and 60% growth — unaudited, on its own benchmarks, before any public filing" smuggles in "unaudited" and conflates annualized revenue with ARR before the update gives permission. That is how a useful angle becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "unaudited" is not in the update. Private and unpublished does not automatically mean unaudited; that word needs evidence or it comes out.
"$3B ARR" overstates the supplied fact, which is "$3B in annualized revenue." A does ask the right question later, but the headline already made the mistake.

"Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" leans on auditability the update does not actually state. Open license and fine-tuning are not the same thing as audit logging or regulatory audit rights.
Angle 3 jams together revenue, benchmarks, private-company status, and IPO signaling. There is a cleaner self-benchmarking story hiding there, but A buries it under financial-accountability fog.
gaps_in_B: "would rather host a model than call one" is a sharp line, but hosting is an inference from open license/fine-tuning, not a stated fact. Keep it as a question unless deployment terms are confirmed.
"$62B last-round mark" may be too specific. The update says last valued at $62B, not whether that mark came from a primary round, secondary tender, or other valuation event.

"open weights mean third parties can begin reproducing them immediately" is plausible from open-sourcing, but the set should verify that the release includes weights and enough evaluation detail to reproduce benchmarks.
The fourth angle admits "No urgent hook." Honest, but it means this is analysis inventory, not the first same-day pitch unless an exec or analyst proof point is unusually strong.
